entry.title: Was I wrong about fitness surfaces? Reply to reply to reply to Dembski

link.title: Was I wrong about fitness surfaces? Reply to reply to reply to Dembski

entry.content:
Not too long ago I became aware that William Dembski had a new article (here) in the BIO-Complexity (the Discovery Institute’s house journal). And that a section of that article disputed my statements about smooth fitness landscapes (or fitness surfaces).

He is replying to a post by me here at Panda’s Thumb on 6 February 2025 (here). He and Robert Marks (and also Winston Ewert) had argued that there was a Conservation of Information law, that showed that when information gets into genomes, it must have already existed elsewhere. They said that this was even true when natural evolutionary processes put adaptive information into the genome – it must have already existed, for example, in the fitness landscape.

Their argument (which can be seen here and here) uses the concept of “active information”. For situations in which there is a population evolving on a fitness landscape, active information can include the information embodied in the assignment of fitnesses to genotypes.

Dembski, in his BIO-Complexity paper, summarizes my arguments thusly:

  1. Real-life biological evolution requires smooth fitness landscapes.
  2. Physics and chemistry guarantee that real-life fitness landscapes are smooth.
  3. Any probability estimates of smooth fitness landscapes among the totality of fitness landscapes are therefore irrelevant.
  4. No-free-lunch theorems hold for the totality of fitness landscapes, both smooth and non-smooth.
  5. No-free-lunch theorems therefore do not apply to real-life biological evolution.
  6. Conservation of information is equivalent to no freelunch, so conservation of information is likewise irrelevant to real-life biological evolution.

He argues that there are exceptions to all fitness landscapes being smooth, and that I have conflated the No Free Lunch argument with his Conservation of Information argument, and that the latter is his essential argument.

Let’s look at his refutation in some detail:

We’ll consider a simple case of evolution. A case where we have a set of genotypes, and each possible one has a fitness. Where there is a simple form of mutation which changes a genotype by substituting one base for another at one of the sites of the genotype. The mapping between genotype and fitness is the fitness landscape.

Dembski’s 2002 argument

If we go back to his 2002 book, Dembski poses tne question of whether “algorithms” such as natural selection can explain the origin of Complex Specified information. He argues (on page 149) that

Algorithms and natural laws are in principle incapable of explaining the origin of CSI. To be sure, algorithms and natural laws can explain the flow of CSI. Indeed, algorithms and natural laws are ideal for transmitting already existing CSI.

Taking that position, in the case of a fitness landscape, if natural selection and other evolutionary processes achieve an increase in fitness great enough to be counted as Complex Specified Information, that information must be already existing in the form of the fitness landscape (or as he called them in 2002, fitness functions).

Dembski concludes (p. 195), for the case of an evolutionary algorithm, that it

has borrowed specified complexity
from a higher-order phase space, namely, the phase space of fitness functions.

Where No Free Lunch comes in

For all possible genotypes (say 3 billion bases in a hapoid genome, with each base being one of A, C, G or T) the fitness is a nonnegative real number. The set of all possible combinations of fitnesses is a very big space, and that does not even consider variation in the length of the genome.

To consider how much specified information comes from the particular fitness landscape, we need to know the probabilities of all possible combinations of fitnesses. That is a very big space.

A much smaller and simpler space is the one considered by Wolpert and Macready in their No Free Lunch theorem (here). They consider one assignment of fitnesses to all of the possible sequences, and then permute those assignments in all possible ways. Their No Free Lunch theorem shows that, averaged over all of these assignments, when they were weighted equally and the search algorithm looked at K genotypes in all, the success of search for higher fitnesses would be no better than choosing the best out of arandomly chosen K genotypes.

This means that when the search algorithm found success by moving one step in a particular direction, an algorithm that continues to move further that direction would not help with further gains. When the fitness landscape is equally likely to see any permutation of fitnesses, there is no way to choose any good direction to move.

Strong and unpredictable interactions between sites

In the No Free Lunch case, there are also typically very strong and unpredictable interactions between sites. If we have two different sites in the genome, and find a favorable substitution at each of them, what happens when both of these substitutions have occurred? The combination of them is yet another haploid genome, so that there is no way to predict what the fitness will be when both changes have occurred.

Is the No Free Lunch case the worst case for evolution?

The point of invoking the No Free Lunch theorem is to show a situation in which evolutionary change will do not better than a search that looked at the same number of genotypes, but picked at random from all possible genotypes. Is that case one in which no progress is made? Some progress will be made. By finding the highest fitness among K genotypes, we do put some functional information into the organism’s genome.

K+L simulations stalling on local peaks

NOTE:

  1. Specification increases at each step, whether in a white-noise surface or in a smooth one.
  2. Kauffman and Levin (?) simulatiom
  3. So both within-landscape and in choice of landscapes information is gained.
  4. We are stuck with the rules of physics.

Is intelligence required?

Is there a predisposition to CSI in real fitness functions

What did I say about physics and fitness landscapes?

A strawman, but no refutation

No Free Lunch versus conservation of information

================================================================================================

================================================================================================

oops, folks. Have not written most of post yet. Will be reposted in a day or two. Right now just some quoted stuff from Dembski, not all of which will be in the final post.

======================================== Dembski’s critique:

By themselves, the no-free-lunch theorems do not refute Darwinism, nor have I ever claimed that they do. Yes, I wrote a book titled No Free Lunch (pub lished in 2002) that used the no-free-lunch theorems as a springboard to critically re-examine the power of the Darwinian mechanism in explaining biological complexity and from there to argue that design is a better expla nation of biological complexity. Yet Darwinian critics of conservation of information have ever since conflated Volume 2025 | Issue 2 | Page 32 conservation of information with no free lunch, arguing The Law of Conservation of Information (rightly) that no free lunch fails to refute Darwinism, but then claiming (wrongly) that conservation of information is identical with no free lunch and thus likewise fails. Hence the fallacy of false equivalence, in which these critics refute what was not contested and then claim that the refutation refutes something else. Joseph Felsenstein is a case in point, but he is rep resentative of Jason Rosenhouse, the late Mark Perakh, Richard Wein, Erik Tellgren, Ole H¨aggstr¨om, and the duo of Wesley Elsberry and Jeffrey Shallit.43 The no free-lunch theorems show that any algorithm averaged over fitness landscapes (Felsenstein calls them “fitness surfaces”) is equivalent to any other algorithm when aver aged in this way. It then follows that any such averaged algorithm is equivalent to blind search. In the statement of these theorems, no restriction is placed on the fitness landscapes. Thus they can be completely jagged, with one member of the configuration space having a com pletely different fitness value from an immediate neighbor. Most fitness landscapes would thus be like hash functions in cryptography (Felsenstein describes them as “white noise fitness surfaces”) where the slightest change in an input completely alters the numerical output [42]. Now Felsenstein’s point is that such jagged fitness landscapes, as allowed by no-free-lunch theorems, violate biological reality. The fitness landscapes conducive to evolvability, such as might characterize how genotypes promote reproductive success, must, according to him, be smooth. Why? Because of physics. Thus he remarks: [I]t seems reasonable that physics itself predis poses fitness surfaces to be smooth. After all, the forces of physics tend to be local in time and space and to lose influence with greater distance. If I gesture with my fingers, there is hardly any effect on objects at a distance. The floor of our room does not collapse, nor does the ceiling cave in. Different objects are scarcely affected by each other.44 The problems with this reasoning are numerous. In the first place, physics does have a place for precipitous and even nonlocal effects. Quantum entanglement is instan taneous and unaffected by distance. Phase transitions in nonlinear dynamics may produce radical changes in the behavior of a system with but the slightest change in a parameter. Felsenstein’s argument is based on folk physics, not modern physics and as such is unconvincing. 43See guments,” Joseph Felsenstein, Panda’s “Conservation Thumb (February 6, of Ar 2025): https://pandasthumb.org/archives/2025/02/Conservation of-arguments.html (last accessed February 24, 2025). For the criticisms by Rosenhouse et al., see the relevant links in the Felsenstein article. 44Felsenstein, “Conservation of Arguments.” Leaving aside physics, Felsenstein cites mutational effects as empirical evidence for smoothness of fitness landscapes. In fact, he defines smoothness to mean that small mutational changes lead to small functional changes. According to Felsenstein, the empirical evidence shows that single mutations typically result in small, pre dictable changes rather than chaotic, random effects. But smoothness in this sense admits striking exceptions. A host of serious genetic diseases such as sickle cell ane mia, phenylketonuria, and Tay-Sachs disease all result from single point mutations. Nonsense mutations, where a single nucleotide substitution produces a stop codon within a coding sequence, cause premature termination of protein synthesis, sometimes with lethal consequences. Frameshift mutations, which may be caused by a single nucleotide insertion or deletion, completely disrupt pro tein synthesis downstream of the mutation, often with huge consequences. And even single amino-acid substitu tions caused by single nucleotide substitutions can have drastic effects, depending on the location and the role of the protein. Thus, contrary to Felsenstein’s smoothness hypothesis, minor genetic change can and does lead to a catastrophic loss of function. According to Bill Gates, “DNA is like a computer pro gram but far, far more advanced than any software ever created” [43, p. 188]. But, as we just saw, smoothness admits exceptions with digital codes in cells. Likewise, it admits exceptions with digital codes in computer soft ware. In fact, it is fairer to say that smoothness is the exception rather than the rule in computer programs. Indeed, one stray letter, one comma out of place, can sub vert a program, preventing it from achieving its objective, if it even functions at all. Evolutionists never define smoothness of fitness land scapes with anything like mathematical precision. But let us say that smoothness could be made mathemati cally precise and that for biological evolution to work it requires smooth fitness landscapes. Smoothness, even then, cannot guarantee the evolvability needed for Dar winian theory to be successful. Smoothness has to mean something like that by moving to near neighbors, fitness should not change drastically. Empirical evidence from some genetic diseases, as noted, contradicts smoothness in this sense. But even if smoothness could be said to hold most of the time, it says nothing about regions of a biological configuration space where fitness is zero. Indeed, fitness landscapes that are zero over such regions are as smooth as they can be over those regions. More over, if fitness is zero over sufficiently vast regions of a configuration space, the viable candidates for evolu tion will be sparsely distributed, drastically curtailing evolvability. Additionally, smoothness does nothing to assuage the problem of multiple local optima where fitness cannot be improved by gradual evolution. In this case, evolution Volume 2025 | Issue 2 | Page 33 The Law of Conservation of Information gets stuck because it cannot break away from those local optima, there being no gradual way for fitness to improve. Fortunately, evolution allows for more radical genetic events than point mutations, such as inversions, translocations, deletions, and duplications. But in that case, smoothness loses its hold because, with such large scale structural changes, all bets are off as to what effect they may have on evolution. Smoothness is essentially a continuity condition, and continuity is always a matter of small local changes in an independent variable leading to small changes in a dependent variable. Smoothness says nothing about how the dependent variable may change in response to large-scale non-local changes in the independent variable. And genetics allows such changes. Felsenstein’s argument can thus be summarized as follows:

  1. Real-life biological evolution requires smooth fit ness landscapes.
  2. Physics and chemistry guarantee that real-life fit ness landscapes are smooth.
  3. Any probability estimates of smooth fitness land scapes among the totality of fitness landscapes are therefore irrelevant.
  4. No-free-lunch theorems hold for the totality of fit ness landscapes, both smooth and non-smooth.
  5. No-free-lunch theorems therefore do not apply to real-life biological evolution.
  6. Conservation of information is equivalent to no free lunch, so conservation of information is likewise irrelevant to real-life biological evolution. Felsenstein’s argument is problematic for more than just point 6. As we’ve seen, smoothness as applied to fitness landscapes in evolution is questionable on both theoretical and empirical grounds. Points 1 to 3 are therefore problematic. But even granting points 1 to 5, the falsity point 6 means conservation of information puts design back in the running in biology. Even though Felsenstein mistakenly conflates of the two, conservation of information is distinct from no free lunch. Whatever fitness landscapes and other conditions on evolvability are needed to bring about a system like Douglas Axe’s beta-lactamase, if those conditions raise the probability of success of evolving such a system, those conditions themselves become highly improbable and require expla nation.

The baseline probability for a system like beta lactamase is indeed small because of the radical con tingency and numerous degrees of freedom of its peptide constituents (see Subsection 10.4). Evolvability therefore grinds to a halt unless it can overcome these otherwise inherent improbabilities (just as, in Section 8, Dawkins’ hill-climbing algorithm overcame the inherent improba bility of generating by purely random means the target phrase METHINKS IT IS LIKE A WEASEL). Conser vation of information tracks the probabilistic cost of overcoming improbability. As such, conservation of infor mation is not concerned with the details of how evolution does it. In particular, it is irrelevant if smooth fitness landscapes, however these are defined, are improbable within a wider class of fitness landscapes, and whether a no-free-lunch theorem exists or does not exist to tease apart the fitness landscapes that facilitate evolution from those that do not.

The fundamental problem with Felsenstein’s critique of conservation of information is this: it is simply irrel evant whether no-free-lunch theorems undercut or fail to undercut Darwinian evolution. What is relevant is that no-free-lunch theorems have no way to undercut conservation of information. Conflating the two is ille gitimate. True, in the history of scientific discovery, no free lunch preceded and provided inspiration for conser vation of information. No free lunch showed that when averaged over fitness landscapes, no search algorithm outperformed any other. But some search algorithms do outperform others for given problems. What, then, empowers some algorithms to outperform others? The short answer: information.

No free lunch raises the right question but by itself does not answer it. The answer depends on conservation of information. Conservation of information characterizes the performance of algorithms in terms of their proba bility of successfully carrying out searches (the bigger the probability, the better the performance). The very statement of the Law of Conservation of Information, by being framed strictly in terms of probabilities, contains no reference to fitness landscapes and in no way depends on the statements or proofs of the no-free-lunch theo rems. That is not to say that fitness may not arise in some applications of conservation of information. Ap pendix 2, for instance, in recapping previously proven conservation-of-information theorems, states a fitness theoretic conservation-of-information theorem. But in any discussions of evolvability, conservation of informa tion can be considered on its own terms irrespective of no free lunch

entry.title: Jared Diamond: What if Darwin had died in childbirth&quest;

link.title: Jared Diamond: What if Darwin had died in childbirth&quest;

entry.content:
I recently listened to Jared Diamond interviewed on an episode of The Michael Shermer Show: How Much Can One Person Change History? Diamond is probably best known for his book Guns, Germs, and Steel, which I had read when it came out. His newest book, published this fall, is Profits, Prophets, Coaches, and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Matter? The content of the book is well summarized in the Shermer Show and also reflected accurately in the titles. That said, when someone as bright as Diamond wonders about Darwin, I have to take notice, so I picked up the book and read it, followed by three reviews, in the Times, the Guardian, and the Globe and Mail. The Globe and Mail article was favorable, the Guardian article mixed, and the Times article properly critical but sometimes perhaps a bit catty.

Before we get to Darwin, let us back up a little bit and discuss what Diamond calls the Hamlet test.

Early on in the book, Diamond proposes the Hamlet test as a means to decide whether some historical event could have taken place without a specific individual. He concludes that to write a play in Elizabethan England, you had to have a connection with a theater company. Very few people (Marlowe? Jonson?) had such connections, and Diamond thinks that those other than Shakespeare were not up to writing a play as good as Hamlet. Marlowe’s and Jonson’s plays are rarely performed today; I have read Tamburlaine but never seen a play by either Marlowe or Jonson. Hence, the Hamlet test: Remove Shakespeare, and no Hamlet. Thus, Diamond asks, if you remove a person from history, would history be different? Apply the Hamlet test and find out. (The Guardian’s reviewer, Stephen Poole, notes a devil in the detail that Marlowe was killed at the age of 29, or 10 years younger than Shakespeare was when he wrote Hamlet. Maybe in 10 years Marlowe would have been capable of writing a play as great as Hamlet.)

Darwin at last: Michael Shermer asks about Darwin at approximately the 38-min mark in the interview. Citing Frank Sulloway, he notes that Darwin was already investigating a voyage to the Canary Islands when he agreed to travel on the Beagle. Evolution was in the air, but (to use Pasteur’s phrase) Darwin had the only prepared mind. Diamond claims that

the breakthrough began with Charles Darwin's 1859 book On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection. That book amassed half a dozen lines of overwhelming evidence for evolution, based on fossils, biogeography, geographic variation, anatomy, embryology, taxonomy and domestication. Darwin thereby ‘jump-started’ the conversion of biologists, and of much of the broad public, to accept evolution as a fact, and natural selection's role as a driving force.

Diamond goes on to anticipate your objections by claiming that Darwin “stood out” by stressing natural selection and unlike Alfred Russel Wallace recognized the role of sexual selection. “Hence I think,” says Diamond, “that a world without Darwin might have been a different world, albeit still a world accepting evolution as a fact.”

That conclusion seems fairly weak. Without Darwin, we would not have been deprived of a theory of natural selection; Wallace would have provided it (if not Patrick Matthew, though that is a longshot). Would scientific progress in and public acceptance of evolution have slowed and by how much, if Darwin had died of smallpox at age 6? What would evolutionary biology be like today? What other scientists actually changed the history of science? What do readers think?

Just for the record, I have singled out Diamond’s examination of Darwin’s contribution, which appears in an Epilogue. There is much more to the book than the Hamlet test. I am not expert enough to know whether his overall approach is defensible. Sometimes his conclusion is an unequivocal maybe.

And finally, sort of an appendix: Diamond convinces me that absolutely nothing would have changed if Gregor Mendel had not performed his experiments on peas. Mendel’s work was discovered only after several later botanists had independently performed similar experiments. Diamond wonders why no one besides Mendel had thought of such simple experiments and notes that “breakthroughs in science also require efforts by leaders to disseminate their discoveries.” I was underwhelmed, at best.

entry.title: When smart people believe stupid things

link.title: When smart people believe stupid things

entry.content:
A penpal of mine, Scott Goodman, recently asked the following question:

What is the psychology behind contrarian belief systems? Having been involved in this now for some 30 years, I have concluded, as have others, that this phenomenon of latching on to a nonsense belief and defending it to the death against all reason is, at its root, psychologically and emotionally driven. And it certainly isn’t limited to creationism. Across the board, from climate change denial to anti-vaccine hysteria to insisting that elections are rigged, I believe the same thing is at work. Consider the characteristics:

  • Impervious to facts or logic. The facts simply must be wrong.
  • A desire to focus on the best and most robust scientific (or political) explanations.
  • Along with that, attacking the most prominent scientists; Darwin, Einstein, etc.
  • And several other characteristics that one might describe.

I throw this out to the group because it might point to finding more effective ways of combatting all of this nonsense. Clearly, facts are water off a duck’s back to creationists and other science deniers. They have a mental force field to keep facts and logic out. To me the question becomes, “What is the emotional payoff for this behaviour?” It appears to be overwhelming and compelling for those who adopt this way of thinking.

A psychiatrist, to whom the question was originally directed, responded:

TBH, I don’t know if I have a good answer to this question, even though it is at least adjacent to my field of expertise. But I do have thoughts.

It is easy to presume that we, as a species, are motivated to seek the truth because we are unusually good at finding the truth. However, it is more likely that we, like every other organism possessed of a degree of sentience, are primarily motivated to do whatever feels good. If that results in beliefs that align with reality, fine. But beliefs do not necessarily align with reality.

I wonder if some of us get an unusual amount of pleasure from learning what is true, and that this overrides whatever discomfort or displeasure accompanies this knowledge. This may not be the case for creationists and other denialists, for whom abandoning their false beliefs exacts a psychological cost they are not motivated to pay.

I’ve become a bit cynical in my time engaging in this debate, having seen so few people ever change their position despite having enough intelligence and knowledge to understand why they are wrong, and being presented evidence by people who are able to communicate very effectively.

At this point, I don’t think the priority is to convince people to change their minds. Rather, it ought to be to get denialists out of positions of influence and power – and keep them out. That is particularly the case in the US at this time.

Biologist John Harshman noted,

All the people I know personally, or online, who were de-programmed from creationism began by studying science and noticing that creationism (that is, biblical literalism) didn’t make sense when compared to the data. Obviously this doesn’t work for everyone, since, e.g., Kurt Wise is still a creationist.

John Wilkins, a philosopher of biology, recommended his article, Are Creationists Rational?, of which I reproduce the abstract:

Creationism is usually regarded as an irrational set of beliefs. In this paper I propose that the best way to understand why individual learners settle on any mature set of beliefs is to see that as the developmental outcome of a series of “fast and frugal” boundedly rational inferences rather than as a rejection of reason. This applies to those whose views are opposed to science in general. A bounded rationality model of belief choices both serves to explain the fact that folk traditions tend to converge on “anti-modernity”, and to act as a default hypothesis, deviations from which we can use to identify other, arational, influences such as social psychological, economic and individual dispositions. I propose some educational and public policy strategies that might decrease the proportion of learners who find creationism and anti-science in general a rational choice.

And chemist Paul Braterman offered this reference:

Stephan Lewandowski and colleagues have put together a great deal of work about dealing with disinformation, e.g., The Debunking Handbook, 2020, with over a hundred references. It becomes much more difficult when the erroneous belief is part of an individual’s identity, such as beliefs linked to religion (as creationism invariably is, apart from a few philosophers), or tribal loyalty, as in the collective rejection of elitism, including scientific authority.

I will leave further discussion to the Comments.

entry.title: Williamstown secret deal may get a free fire station for the Ark

link.title: Williamstown secret deal may get a free fire station for the Ark

entry.content:
Will the Ark Park get a free fire station from the City of Williamstown? Is the Ark going to announce a Tower of Babel ride soon (and get more tax incentives)?

Back on January 8, 2026, the acting Mayor of Williamstown, Kentucky, Dave Henson, had a special meeting/luncheon with Ken Ham and several Answers in Genesis/Ark Encounter officers on the Ark Encounter property. I submitted a Kentucky Open Records Act (KORA) request to Williamstown and received a handful of documents including photographs of the Mayor with Ken Ham and the meeting agenda. The meeting agenda briefly mentions a discussion of a “Fire Department substation” on Eibeck Lane (the employees’ and delivery entrance to the Ark) but nothing specific. Since this wasn’t considered a City Council meeting, nothing appeared to be official.

In early August, I noticed a record in the Grant County News where Ark Development, LLC (an Answers in Genesis shell company) had sold the City of Williamstown an ~1.9 acre property on Eibeck Road for $1. This piqued my curiosity, and I sent a KORA request to the City on August 3, 2026. On August 7, 2026, before the City responded to my open records request, I visited Williamstown in person to look up the exact location and take a photo of the site.

My visit to the County Clerk’s and PVA (Property Evaluation Administrator) offices revealed the exact location of the property on Eibeck Lane. The property is surrounded by Ark Encounter property and is on the Ark’s “employee and delivery entrance” located on the Ark’s private access road. To avoid trespassing, I stopped before entering the Ark’s property and photographed the property from a distance. My photo is attached. Also attached is a Google Maps image showing a pin for the location of the front of the property. You presently cannot access the property without trespassing on Ark property.

On August 11, 2026, I received the KORA package from the City. It revealed that the property is valued at $10,000. The deed records show that the Ark sold the property to Williamstown on March 8, 2018, for $1. Then on July 7, 2022, the City sold the property back to the Ark for $1. Then, on April 23, 2026, the City bought the property again for $1.

There is only one discussion of the property in the minutes of the Williamstown City Council on May 17, 2022 (more than 4 years ago). At this meeting the topic of “Returning of Property Back to Ark that was Supposed to be used for Fire Substation” was discussed. The record states that “Mayor Skinner stated the property was donated to the City in 2012 [he could be mistaken about the date given the deeds provided in the KORA – d.p.] for the purpose of a Fire Substation. Mayor Skinner stated that he and Fire Chief Les Whalen think it is not the proper location for a substation. Some discussion [not recorded – d.p.] occurred.” It then states “Ronnie West made the motion to return the property back to the Ark that was supposed to be used for a Fire Substation. Greg Middleton seconded the motion…. All voted in favor.” And the motion carried.

There is no other information concerning these property transfers in the KORA material I received.

When acting Mayor Henson and the Williamstown City Council have their public meetings, they often go into closed session. The meeting agendas then usually state, “Motion to go into Executive Session pursuant to KRS 61.810(1)(g) discussions regarding a business entity concerning a specific proposal as open discussions would jeopardize the citing, retention or upgrading of the business.”

The full text of KRS 61.810(1)(g) can be found here.

So far this year, the Williamstown City Council meetings have cited KRS 61.810(1)(g) in their agendas on February 2, March 2, May 19, June 1, July 6, July 21, and September 8 (seven times this year). (See all of the Williamstown City Council meeting Agendas here). According to the Kentucky Open Government Coalition website, Kentucky government agencies cannot take final action or vote on binding measures during a closed session. Any formal decision or vote must occur during the open, public portion of the meeting.

The Executive Sessions could be discussing other business entities but given the importance of the Ark to Williamstown politicians and the scarcity of other businesses interested in Williamstown, that is unlikely. Other possible business that the City of Williamstown has been dealing with includes selling/leasing an old gym, a warehouse, and a building formerly owned by Northern Kentucky University. Thus, a minority of the closed sessions could be devoted to these other projects. However, since there is no public record concerning the purchase of the Eibeck Lane property from AIG, some, perhaps a majority, of these closed sessions involve the City and AIG’s interests.

Was the vote, if any, to repurchase the property this year for $1 done in one of these secret “Executive Sessions”? Or was the property somehow purchased without a vote? Was any due diligence conducted to inspect the site for possible environmental or other liabilities? Why is no public record available?

I contacted a reporter from the Grant County News about this matter. She said that Mayor Henson told her, “The property was originally deeded to the City when the Ark Encounter project was initiated, with the intention that it could serve as the site of a future fire department substation. Because the City did not move forward with that use at the time, the property was deeded back to the Ark Encounter. The City is now considering the property for a possible future fire department substation and potentially a training facility. In January, I [the Mayor] asked representatives of the Ark Encounter to deed the property back to the City, and they were pleased to accommodate that request.” There is no public record of the City purchasing this property other than the deed. Everything else was apparently done in secret. Even the cancelled check for $1.00 was not provided to my KORA request.

There is no public record of the decision to reacquire the property, and no vote, no discussion of why it was deemed to not be suitable for a fire station in 2022 (but suddenly the property is or might be suitable in 2026).

Questions for the Mayor and City Council of Williamstown include:

  • Is Williamstown going to build a fire station on the property or not?
  • If not, what are the plans for the property since it is landlocked by Ark property?
  • Since it is surrounded by Ark property, which is private, how can the city and its residents possibly make use of that property?
  • There is no record of any public vote on reacquiring the property. Why?

Interestingly enough, AIG probably could easily raise its own funds to build their own fire station without getting the City to build it or finance it any way. In spite of declining ticket sales, the Ark is afloat in cash from donations. As I write this, Ken Ham has announced a $24 million fundraiser. A day and a half after the announcement, the multi-month fundraiser has already raised more than $2.4 million.

I have long predicted that when the Kentucky Tourism Sales Tax rebate expires, the Ark will change from a for-profit to a non-profit entity to avoid the monthly 50 cents per ticket Safety Fee to Williamstown. In spite of this likelihood, could the City now be planning to construct a firehouse, at City expense, on this property surrounded by Ark property? The Ark has a long record of getting one perk after another from sympathetic government entities. What is the town going to do to replace the per-ticket fee if the Ark becomes a non-profit?

The repeated “Executive Sessions” suggest extensive discussions with Williamstown concerning a proposal with a business entity. Since Crosswater Canyon (the for-profit AIG shell company that enabled the Ark to receive sales tax rebate incentives from Kentucky Tourism) has now received the last of the tax rebate money, perhaps AIG is going ahead with other projects. AIG has discussed “recreating” the Tower of Babel as a ride and/or movie theater since way back when the Ark was in its planning stages. It has been several years since Ken Ham discussed adding a “Tower of Babel” onto the Ark Encounter property. In his 2022 discussion, Ham says, “This project is still several years out, and will require much planning, design work, budgeting, fundraising, Kentucky tourism & permit approvals, etc. long before we formally announce we are moving ahead and can break ground.”

I would not be surprised if there is an attempt to get the Kentucky Tourism Commission to grant new tax incentives for the Tower of Babel “recreation.” In fact, this could explain the odd and possibly misleading presentation that representatives of the Ark made to a Kentucky Legislative Committee on Tourism back in July. At that meeting, the Ark was inexplicably praised as an economic dynamo for Kentucky whereas ticket sales have never matched the Ark’s projections and are, in fact, declining. That meeting may have been a way to soften up Kentucky officials for further breaks for AIG enterprises.

Another possibility is that AIG is waiting for a new Governor, of either party, who would be more likely to back a project with ties to Christian Nationalism. Members of the Legislature from Northern Kentucky are dominated by conservative, Christian Nationalists. Governor Andy Beshear’s term will end in December, 2027. Ken Ham has attacked Beshear repeatedly on Facebook and other social media for the Governor’s positions on social issues and has repeatedly complained that the Governor has never visited the Ark or Creation Museum.
entry.summary: PVA property plot of the possible future Williamstown fire station. Note that it is surrounded by Ark property and only accessible via the Ark’s service road. Will the Ark Park get a free fire station from the City of Williamstown? Is the Ark going to announce a Tower of Babel ride soon (and get more tax incentives)? Back on January 8, 2026, the acting Mayor of Williamstown, Kentucky, Dave Henson, had a special meeting/luncheon with Ken Ham and several Answers in Genesis/Ark Encounter officers on the Ark Encounter property. I submitted a Kentucky Open Records Act (KORA) request to Williamstown and received a handful of documents including photographs of the Mayor with Ken Ham and the meeting agenda. The meeting agenda briefly mentions a discussion of a “Fire Department substation” on Eibeck Lane (the employees’ and delivery entrance to the Ark) but nothing specific. Since this wasn’t considered a City Council meeting, nothing appeared to be official. In early August, I noticed a record in the Grant County News where Ark Development, LLC (an Answers in Genesis shell company) had sold the City of Williamstown an ~1.9 acre property on Eibeck Road for $1. This piqued my curiosity, and I sent a KORA request to the City on August 3, 2026. On August 7, 2026, before the City responded to my open records request, I visited Williamstown in person to look up the exact location and take a photo of the site.

entry.title: Publisher recalls book that misquotes Michael Behe

link.title: Publisher recalls book that misquotes Michael Behe

entry.content:
A report in Retraction Watch, University press removes book about intelligent design for misquoting ID proponent, reported, “New York University Press is pulling all copies of a book about intelligent design after the author falsely quoted another scholar in the work.” The book is Designer Science: A History of Intelligent Design in America, by C.W. Howell. I was slightly taken aback by the word falsely, where inaccurately might have held less baggage. At any rate, Retraction Watch says,

The misquote stemmed from a passage in a court ruling Howell “mistakenly” read as a direct quote from Behe and attributed as such, he told us. Howell writes about the intersection of faith and science, and serves as an academic director for the C.S. Lewis Foundation.

The book has been pulled from the market and does not appear on Amazon. The Press will presumably reissue the book after the error has been corrected. I consider that beyond principled: I consider the the misquotation a minor error (all books have errors, even mine). I would have treated it like an error in a published paper and simply issued an erratum, posted the erratum on the publisher’s and my web pages, and probably tried to get Amazon to follow suit.

Though not listed on Amazon, the book is still listed in Publishers Weekly, which gave it a favorable but not starred review. Curious, I looked it up and skimmed the Introduction. It is well and clearly written, and notes that the damage done by intelligent-design creationism is still with us:

While ID’s community of supporters is still active–especially on the internet–in the media and culture at large, it is generally perceived today as defunct, and virtually all prior scholarly work on intelligent design ends with the Dover case from 2005. But intelligent design did not disappear. This book makes the case that its legacy is far more significant than we might think. Even though it did fail to achieve its goal of remaking contemporary science, intelligent design both planted the seeds and nurtured the growth of extreme skepticism in the world of US conservatism, a trend that has continued to grow ever since, sprouting in contemporary antivaccine movements and climate change denialism, among other things. We are all grappling today with intelligent design’s legacy, even when we are not directly talking about its serious intellectual content and its highly technical scientific attacks on Darwin.

After observing that he is closest to a theistic evolutionist, Howell, a historian with a PhD from Duke University, says,

... I have tried my best to present ID in a critical but fair light–not to disprove it (or prove it) but simply to understand it and its supporters. It is my hope that this book will, to appropriate Darwin’s phrase about origins, “throw light” on a movement that exerted, and still does exert, great influence on life in the US and that it will help illuminate the beliefs, politics, and effects of ID such as they were and are in the late twentieth and early twenty-first century.

I will look forward to this book when it is finally reissued.

entry.title: Loxodonta cyclotis
entry.content:
Photography Contest.

Joel Eissenberg, Honorable Mention.
entry.summary: Photography Contest. Joel Eissenberg, Honorable Mention. Loxodonta cyclotis – African elephant. Dr. Eissenberg writes, "Image taken at Roger Williams Park Zoo in Providence RI. Elephants have wrinkled skin composed of a dense network of fractures that helps them survive in hot climates. The deep creases form a web of microvalleys that trap moisture, allowing their skin to retain up to ten times more water than a smooth surface. This trapped moisture cools them through evaporation."
